catalog_citation: Daniels, Don R. 2010. A preliminary phonological history of the Sogeram languages of Papua New Guinea. Oceanic Linguistics 49(1): 163-193. doi:10.1353/ol.0.0068
catalog_locator: p. 168, section 2 PROTO-SOGERAM, the sentence directly below phoneme inventory (1); supporting restatement p. 175, section 4.1.2 Vowel centering.
catalog_quote: p. 168: "Stress is almost always word-final in the daughter languages, and it was probably also word-final in PSOG. The central vowel /ɨ/ behaves as a neutral vowel in the family, arising paragogically and epenthetically in many situations (cf. 3.1.2, 3.1.4, and 4.4.1), and being the result of any vowel-centering processes (such as 4.1.2. and 5.2.4)." p. 175 (4.1.2 Vowel centering): "Unrounded vowels in closed penults centered to /ɨ/ when followed by open ultimas; the fact that PSOG probably had word-final stress helps motivate this change."
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.quote: p. 168: "Stress is almost always word-final in the daughter languages, and it was probably also word-final in PSOG." p. 175 (4.1.2 Vowel centering): "Unrounded vowels in closed penults centered to /ɨ/ when followed by open ultimas; the fact that PSOG probably had word-final stress helps motivate this change." p. 177 (4.3.1): "While this innovation is not a bizarre phonetic development, the fact that these languages probably had word-final stress makes it a little peculiar."

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Held PDF (Project MUSE, title page: 'A Preliminary Phonological History of the Sogeram Languages', Don R. Daniels, Oceanic Linguistics 49(1), June 2010, pp. 163-193) and the extraction. All three quoted sentences are present verbatim at the stated locators, re-checked against the PDF with extracted text/-l: p. 7 = printed p. 168, section 2 PROTO-SOGERAM, directly under inventory (1): 'Stress is almost always word-final in the daughter languages, and it was probably also word-final in PSOG.' p. 14 = p. 175, 4.1.2 Vowel centering: 'Unrounded vowels in closed penults centered to /ɨ/ when followed by open ultimas; the fact that PSOG probably had word-final stress helps motivate this change.' p.…
new_statements.relation_note: Nend has no catalog record and no existing statements, so there is nothing to agree or disagree with; this is the first placement statement held by the project, and only as a family-wide generalization. It is consistent with the one accented form in Harris 1990 (e'ka 'slice', accent on the final syllable of a disyllable, noted in the 2026-09-17 check of this folder) and with Harris's remark that Nend does not use accent to mark contrast.
new_statements.rule_in_words: A family-level generalization, not a Nend-specific description: stress falls on the last syllable of the word in nearly all Sogeram daughter languages (Nend among them) and is reconstructed as word-final for Proto-Sogeram. The article has no phonology/suprasegmental section for Nend; its Nend section (3.1, pp. 172-174) treats only segmental changes and never mentions stress.
new_statements.exceptions: 'almost always' word-final in the daughter languages; no exceptions or specific languages named, and no statement singles out Nend either way.
new_statements.identity_note: Daniels 2010 fieldwork was in Kwaringri (southern Nend village); Daniels 2020 relies mainly on Kyle Harris's northern (Pasinkap) data and notes North/South dialect differences in segmental changes. Neither stress remark is dialect-specific, and neither is about Nend in particular.

sources.note: Section 0.4 'Phonology of Nend' (p. 80) is only a phoneme inventory (24 consonants, 6 vowels). No statement of where stress falls anywhere in the 83 pages. Accent is presupposed: 0.5.3 Vowel Harmony (p. 81) 'When the vowel in the accented syllable is [+high], the front and back [-high] vowels become [+high].. the verb e'ka 'slice'' (accent mark before the 2nd syllable in this single example); 2.4.2.7 (p. 101) 'Nend does not use accent or intonation to mark contrastiveness.' Nothing else on stress, tone or pitch.

A survey-level impression from wordlist elicitation, not a prosodic analysis.
